name: Charleston Ghosts
description: A self-guided evening walk through the documented history and ghost legends of Charleston's Historic District.

stops.name: The Battery, White Point Garden

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on East Battery Street along White Point Garden, facing the harbor.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on East Battery Street along White Point Garden, where cannon from the Civil War era still point out toward the harbor. The battery was built as a defensive wall and later became the city's grand seafront promenade. During the Civil War, the fortification was an active Confederate defense line, and families watched shells pass over their homes while sheltering in basements across the street. The documented history of the wall and its guns is real and well recorded. The stories told around this stretch are legend, whispered by families who say they hear drums and marching feet on foggy evenings. Keep the walker on the public sidewalk, and keep the legend labeled as legend. The documented history here is clear and well sourced, and the stories that surround it are folklore, told by visitors and by the people who live nearby. The walker who pauses on the public sidewalk can take in both layers at once, the record and the legend, and can leave knowing which is which.

stops.name: St. Michael's Church

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on Meeting Street in front of St. Michael's Church, beside the churchyard fence.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on Meeting Street, in front of St. Michael's Church and beside its churchyard fence. St. Michael's is one of Charleston's oldest churches, begun in 1751, and its steeple has guided ships into the harbor for more than two centuries. The documented history of the church, including its construction and its bells, is real and well sourced. The churchyard holds graves of the city's early citizens, and visitors sometimes say they hear footsteps among the gravestones after dark. Those stories are local legend, not documented fact. The walker stands on the public sidewalk, and the churchyard stays behind its fence. The documented history here is clear and well sourced, and the stories that surround it are folklore, told by visitors and by the people who live nearby. The walker who pauses on the public sidewalk can take in both layers at once, the record and the legend, and can leave knowing which is which.

stops.name: Old Exchange Building

viewpoint.description: Public sidewalk on East Bay Street in front of the Old Exchange Building, beside the columns.

stops.narration: You are standing on the public sidewalk on East Bay Street, in front of the Old Exchange Building beside its grand columns. The Exchange was built in 1771 as Charleston's customs house, town hall, and slave market—a place where the city's commerce and its cruelty met. Enslaved people were sold here, and the documented record of that trade is part of Charleston's history that cannot be softened. During the Revolution, the Exchange held American prisoners, and later its cellars held gunpowder. Visitors who say they hear chains in the basement are telling local legend. The walker stays on the public sidewalk, where the history speaks for itself without needing ghosts. The documented history here is clear and well sourced, and the stories that surround it are folklore, told by visitors and by the people who live nearby. The walker who pauses on the public sidewalk can take in both layers at once, the record and the legend, and can leave knowing which is which.
